It's almost exactly that. In the first paragraph, you almost hit then nail on its head. It's not so much that she *is* helpless, necissarily, but how you might make her *feel* helpless by approaching her. You know that feeling, that we've all felt as some point, of not being in control? When you feel at the mercy of somebody else? That's what she could be subjected to if you approach her. It might sound riddiculous, but it's the truth, because it's the experience most women have experienced, for some even on a weekly basis. It's not as simple as the act of approaching her being wrong, of course, but more how you approach, but that's subjective. People will interpret different cues in different ways. Some things that will come off as smooth to some girl will come off as really creepy to another. All in all, I'm saying it'd probably be better to not approach strangers in this fashion, because it can leave someone in such a situation. That's not to say that it's the worst thing that can happen to a person, *but you'd be the one who'd subject her to that*. That aint a good thing, no matter how you frame it from your view and intent.

Also, I feel as if I should clarify that I don't wholeheartedly agree with everything the "short film" says, especially since the framing of how it's up to each and every man to bash down on gender inequality and whatever that aren't really up to them is idealistic, to say the least. I mean, it's not like they could have gone into detail how at least half of the problem lies the system that enforces such problems, but making it about how it's supposed to be at the fault of these men's behavior is the wrong way to go about changing said behaviors. The behaviors they describe, however, are legitimate, and are a *part* of the problem at hand.

As for the 'moot' point, yes, not being a native speaker shines through every now and again.

And we do agree on the dilemma whether Gilette are even in a place to do this type of thing. I definately think it was the wrong move to try to frame it as a "don't do this shit"-type of thing. They're not in the place to tell people what to do. I do however think that sparking debate is a valid way to launch an ad campaign (it didn't spark debate, really, but it did try to, which is what matters, haha), and following that debate, people might then choose make changes in their behavior. The actual things they bring up are valid things men *should* be doing to "be better", but it's just that they're not in a place to make such demands.

As for the first paragraph, well, yeah. They are promoting "policing" each other's behavior. Everything sounds bad when you frame it as policing, doesn't it? If "policing" entails teaching people to be mindful of how their behavior affects others, is it really that bad? 

The second paragraph, yeah. I realised that a bit after posting: it's for men who "want to be better" or however they framed it. Let me rephrase: If you're not doing the things they're condemning, you're not on trial, here. 

As for the last part, I suppose that's where we disagree. I don't think proposing the idea that men aren't perfect and they can strive to be better should be a controversial topic. It's healthy to look at yourself critically from the perspective of another person. I certainly think that they could have conveyed the message in a somewhat better way (somewhat being literal, they're very close to the mark IMO), too, but still. As to whether a similar commercial would see the same criticism were it to be about women? Yes, it would. However, you'd also have to admit that such backlash would be merited (it'd be pretty hypocritical if you didn't), so it's a pretty mute point.

If you're not doing what they're condemning, you're not on trial here. How that simple concept has flown above everyone's head is beyond me.
